open-question.question: A rule in a project's tracked rule file, and an override in the looped run's preview, names a single-task line of the VS Code extension (`gurita-vscode`) by its recipe's `###` heading. `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` heads its two single-task lines `Single tasks with Opus xHigh` (under Claude Code) and `Single tasks with Opus High` (under Antigravity), names that give the model and effort but not the host. In what form is a shipped single-task line's `###` heading written, for the two lines the file holds and any it gains?
open-question.recommendation: These names are written into tracked rule files and read in the preview, so each states all three things that set one line apart from another. With a Claude Code line at Opus High beside the Antigravity one, model and effort alone no longer name one line, and a pattern that is unique from the start means no later line renames one a rule already names.
open-question.alternative: Every shipped single-task heading names all three of its line's host, model, and effort in human spelling, with the host written in the same form the file's repeated headings use to name theirs, for example `Single task with Opus xHigh (Claude Code)` and `Single task with Opus High (Antigravity)`, and every gained line follows the same pattern. Each name tells the reader of a rule file or a preview exactly what a task will run under, and the pattern stays unique however many lines the file gains, so no addition ever renames an existing line. The names are long to type into a rule file and must be copied exactly; a person's own recipe that replaces one of these headings with a different host, model, or effort keeps a name that now misdescribes it, while a project's tracked rules naming it stay as written. Its host part depends on the form the repeated-heading question settles.

The two headings stay exactly as they stand, `Single tasks with Opus xHigh` under `## Claude Code` and `Single tasks with Opus High` under `## Antigravity`, and every single-task line the file gains is headed in the same pattern, `Single tasks with <Model> <Effort>` in human spelling, naming no host; a gained line whose model and effort match a line under the other host takes the host-naming form the file uses for repeated headings. Nothing in the snippet file changes for these two lines, they are already unique, and the names the maintainer already reads from the file are the names a rule writes. A rule or override never says which host it sends a task to, and the human `Opus` hides that the Antigravity line runs `claude-opus-5-5` while the Claude Code one runs `opus`; a later line repeating a combination under the other host forces a rename that can break rules already written against the bare name, and a person's own recipe replacing one of these headings with another model leaves the name describing a line that no longer runs.

Every shipped single-task heading is built from its line's own literal values, the host binary, the `--model` value, and the `--effort` value, behind a fixed stem, for example `complete-task claude opus xhigh` and `complete-task agy claude-opus-5-5 high`, and every gained line is headed the same way. The name is mechanical: it is read straight off the line it heads, needs no human naming of models or efforts, and distinguishes the two different model ids the two hosts take, so no two combinations can ever share a name. It reads unlike every other heading in the file, the pane, and the preview, and it repeats the line beside it, so an edit to the line that forgets the heading leaves a name that states the wrong values; as with any combination name, a person's own replacement under the same heading makes it misdescribe the line it runs.

Every shipped single-task heading names only its line's host, for example `Single task (Claude Code)` and `Single task (Antigravity)`, with the model and effort left to the line itself, the host written in the form the file's repeated headings use. Short, stable names that a rule file writes easily, and a person's own recipe may swap the model or effort under the same heading without the name becoming untrue. It holds only one shipped line per host: any second combination on one host needs a different naming scheme, renaming the first line and the rules that name it, and a rule no longer shows which model or effort a task gets. Its viability depends on how many lines the shipped-lines question gives each host.

Every shipped single-task heading names the kind of task the line is meant for rather than its combination, for example `Single task (standard)` for the Claude Code Opus `xhigh` line and `Single task (critical)` or another role word for the Antigravity Opus `high` line, the role words chosen once and every gained line taking a role name of its own; no heading names a host, model, or effort. A project's tracked rules name intent, which stays true across people and over time: a person's own recipe file replaces a role's heading with their own host, model, and effort, and a newer model is adopted by editing one line, both without editing any project's rule file and without a name that misdescribes its line. The heading no longer says what a task will run under, so the preview and the pane must show the line itself for a person to see it, and the role words are a new vocabulary to choose and agree on; which roles exist hinges on which combinations the shipped-lines question ships.

Every shipped single-task heading names both the kind of task it is meant for and its line's host, model, and effort, for example `Single task, standard (Opus xHigh, Claude Code)` and `Single task, critical (Opus High, Antigravity)`, and every gained line follows the same pattern. A rule names intent while the heading still tells a reader exactly what the line runs, so both the rule file and the pane read on their own. The longest names to type into a rule file, and the decoupling a role gives is lost: a person's own replacement or a model update under the same heading leaves its combination part untrue, while changing the heading breaks every rule naming it; it carries both a role vocabulary to choose and the host form the repeated-heading question settles.

open-question.question: The design draft `ideas/vscode_extension.md` assigns four things to the drift-gate workflow for the VS Code extension (`gurita-vscode`): its build and tests as Node steps, a check of the fixed console lines it carries against the `## Fixed console lines` table of `docs/skill-reference.md`, a check of its `open_questions.xml` parse against `open_questions.py list --without-alternatives` and `--without-recommendation`, and a check that no `###` heading of `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` repeats. The mission's goal allows such guards to be left out and written up as follow-up work. Which of the four does this mission carry out, and which does it leave out?
open-question.recommendation: The goal names exactly these guards as the parts a first version may leave out, its real test being the maintainer's own trial. CI keeps its single Python toolchain, a drift between plugin and extension fails safe, since an unrecognised first line stops a chain in plain view rather than continuing it, and all four guards are recorded as follow-up work.
open-question.alternative: None of the four is carried out. `.github/workflows/drift-gate.yml` keeps its five steps unchanged, with no Node set up. No test anywhere checks the extension's fixed lines against the `## Fixed console lines` table, its `open_questions.xml` parse against `open_questions.py list --without-alternatives` and `--without-recommendation`, or the snippet file's `###` headings for repeats. All four are written into the follow-up documents under `ideas/` as later work. It is the smallest mission and the one the goal names outright ("the Node steps in the drift-gate workflow and the cross-checks ... may be left out"). The repository's CI keeps a single Python toolchain and gains no action pin to bump by hand, and no test of a directory outside `core/` joins `tests/`. That suits a first version whose real test is the maintainer installing the VSIX and trying it. Every drift the draft gives as its reason for keeping the extension in this repository can now land without notice. A plugin commit that moves one of the fixed lines a looped run reads (`Task completed.`, the scope-gate stop) passes CI and silently stops or misreads the extension's chains. So does a format change that makes the extension's parse select different blocks than the tool's filters, and so does a snippet edit that brings back a repeated heading and makes a fixed-name button ambiguous.

All four are carried out as the draft lays them out. The drift-gate job gains Node steps: a pinned `actions/setup-node` at Node 22, then an install, the extension's build, and its test suite, all run in `gurita-vscode/`. That suite holds three checks of its own. The first reads the extension's carried fixed lines against the `## Fixed console lines` table of `docs/skill-reference.md`. The second runs `core/tools/open_questions.py list --without-alternatives` and `--without-recommendation` with `python3` over the committed question documents under `tests/fixtures/` and compares the blocks they select with the extension's parse. The third checks that no `###` heading of `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` repeats. The existing pytest steps stay as they are. It carries out the draft's design whole. Any plugin commit that moves a fixed line, a filter's meaning, or a heading's uniqueness fails CI in the same commit, and every guard stands beside the code it guards, in the extension's one language and test runner, so the extension's directory holds its whole contract. It is the largest option. A second toolchain enters the repository's one CI job, with a new action SHA to bump by hand and a Node install on every push. The suite also reparses the fixed-line table in TypeScript, beside the Python helpers `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py` already has, so the table has two readers to keep in step. The option holds only if the TypeScript side gets a test runner at all, which the sibling question on TypeScript test coverage settles.

All four are carried out, each guard in the language that already reads its input. The drift-gate job gains Node steps (a pinned `actions/setup-node` at Node 22, then the install, the build, and the extension's test suite), and that suite holds the parse check against `open_questions.py list --without-alternatives` and `--without-recommendation` over the committed fixtures. The fixed-line check and the heading-uniqueness check are written as pytest tests under `tests/`. The fixed-line test reuses the table reading `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py` already does, and the heading test reads `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md`. Both CI pytest runs collect these two tests, at the pinned interpreter and at the 3.9 floor. Every guard is enforced in CI, the same-commit failure the draft asks for, and the two plugin-facing checks reuse the one existing reader of the fixed-line table rather than adding a TypeScript copy of it. Only the check that needs the extension's own parser runs under Node. The extension's guards are spread over two suites and two toolchains: one part lives beside the extension and one in `tests/`, which until now tests only `core/tools/`. CI still gains the Node steps and their pin. The fixed-line test can be written in Python only if the extension carries its lines in a form Python can read, which the sibling question on fixed-line carriage settles.

Two of the four are carried out, as pytest tests under `tests/` that both existing CI runs collect. One checks the extension's carried fixed lines against the `## Fixed console lines` table, reusing the table reading `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py` already does. The other checks that no `###` heading of `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` repeats. The drift-gate workflow gains no Node step: the extension's build and tests run in CI nowhere. The parse check against `open_questions.py list --without-alternatives` and `--without-recommendation` is left out. The Node steps and the parse check are written into the follow-up documents under `ideas/`. It guards the two drifts a plugin change is most likely to cause, a fixed line reworded or a snippet heading duplicated, and makes them fail CI in the same commit. CI keeps its single Python toolchain, gains no new action pin, and needs no step added to the workflow file. The extension's own code goes unchecked in CI: a broken TypeScript build lands without notice, and a change to the question document format that moves what the extension's parse selects is caught only when the maintainer sees a wrong label. `tests/` gains tests of a directory outside `core/`. The fixed-line test can be written in Python only if the extension carries its lines in a form Python can read, which the sibling question on fixed-line carriage settles.

All three cross-checks are written, but only the Python ones are enforced in CI. The fixed-line check and the heading-uniqueness check are pytest tests under `tests/`, collected by both existing CI runs, the fixed-line test reusing the table reading of `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py`. The parse check against `open_questions.py list --without-alternatives` and `--without-recommendation` over the committed fixtures goes into the extension's own Node test suite, which the maintainer runs by hand through nvm.
